narrative: The model estimates a 78% chance that you will leave your job, and that forecast is why the promotion decision went against you. This is a prediction of retention risk, not a judgment of your performance. The strongest signal pushing toward leaving was that you reported having other job opportunities; only about 23% of employees predicted to stay said the same. The next most influential factor was your overall work experience of 6–10 years, which the model treats as a mobility signal, even though it is fairly common among employees predicted to stay. By contrast, your 6–10 years with your current organization pushed in the opposite direction—toward staying—because time already invested in the current workplace is generally a stabilizing signal. So the model sees an experienced employee with outside options, partly anchored by tenure in this organization. The organization should treat the 78% figure as a prompt for a retention conversation, not a final verdict: clarify your career intentions, review what would make a promotion or development path credible, and address satisfaction, recognition, workload and pay where relevant. You should also discuss directly whether you intend to stay and what support or role would keep you engaged.
